title: تَتِمَّةُ حِكَايَةِ الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ الثَّالِثِ وَابْتِدَاءُ حِكَايَةِ الْكُبْرَى
titleEn: The Third Qalandar's Tale Concludes; The Eldest Sister Begins Her Own Tale
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 110–121 (continuing directly from nights-15, whose text breaks off partway through the Third Qalandar's own account), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project's own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition's own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 16 finishes the Third Qalandar's own tale and opens Night 17. Having shot down the brass horseman on the Black Mountain, the qalandar is carried off by an enchanted skiff, thrown into the sea, and swims ashore to a small island, where he secretly enters an underground vault and discovers a jeweler's son hidden there from birth on the strength of a horoscope predicting death at fifteen at the hand of a king's son named 'Ajib — not realizing, until the boy is named, that he himself was that horseman and so is the very man the horoscope warned of. The two live together in hiding for forty days until, on the last, the qalandar's own hand kills the boy by accident, fulfilling the prophecy he had sworn to prevent. He flees, is cast ashore again by chance, is carried by a giant bird to a palace of one-eyed young men, and, pressing them to learn the secret of their nightly rite of ash and mourning, is sent on to a palace of forty princesses; there, after a year of feasting and courtship, curiosity gets the better of him at the one locked door he was told never to open, and the black horse he finds inside flies him to a rooftop where he is blinded in one eye and cast out — the same fate, it is now clear, that made one-eyed men of every host he has met. Blind in one eye himself, wandering, and freshly arrived in Baghdad, he is turned away in his own telling, but the frame catches up with him here: this is the very evening, and the very doorstep, where the caliph Harun al-Rashid — travelling in disguise with Ja'far and Masrur — first met him and the other two one-eyed qalandars. The night closes the frame around all three tales: the lady of the house forgives everyone's earlier bad behavior, the caliph reveals himself the next morning, and the three sisters of the house are asked in turn for their own story; the eldest begins hers — three sisters married, ruined and abandoned by their husbands, reunited in poverty, and setting out together by ship — as dawn cuts Shahrazad off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about the boy's death and about the qalandar's night with each of the princesses, and is translated that way, without euphemism or omission.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةَ عَشَرَ قَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisata ʿashara qāla
sentences.l: Now when it was the sixteenth night, he said,
sentences.n: The archive prints قال here (masculine 'he said'), against the feminine قالت / قٰلَتْ that opened the two preceding nights; kept exactly as printed rather than assimilated to that pattern.

sentences.t: بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ عَجِيبً قَالَ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna ʿajīban qāla li-al-ṣabiyyati
sentences.l: It has reached me, O happy King, that ʿAjīb said to the girl:
sentences.i: It has reached me, O happy King, that ʿAjīb said to the girl:
sentences.n: Until now the narrator has been called only 'the third qalandar.' Here he is named for the first time — ʿAjīb — the very name Night 15's horoscope gave for the king fated to kill the jeweler's son ('ʿAjīb son of Khaṣīb/Khaḍīb'). The text lets the identification speak for itself. عَجِيبً is printed here without the accusative tanwīn's alif; no letter is added or removed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَيَقَّنْتُ أَنِّي قَتَلْتُهُ قُمْتُ وَطَلَعْتُ مِنَ السُّلَّمِ وَرَدَيْتُ التُّرَابَ وَنَظَرْتُ بِعَيْنِي إِلَى الْبَحْرِ فَرَأَيْتُ الْمَرْكَبَ تَشُقُّ الْبَحْرَ ضَارِبَةً الْبَرَّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā tayaqqantu annī qataltuhu qumtu wa-ṭalaʿtu mina al-sullami wa-radaytu al-turāba wa-naẓartu bi-ʿaynī ilā al-baḥri fa-raʾaytu al-markaba tashuqqu al-baḥra ḍāribatan al-barr
sentences.l: And when I made certain that I had killed him, I got up and went up by the ladder, and I put back the earth, and I looked with my eye toward the sea, and I saw the ship cleaving the sea, making for the shore.
sentences.i: When I was sure that I had killed him, I got up, climbed the ladder, and put the earth back in place; then I looked out to sea with my own eyes, and saw the ship cutting through the water, making for the shore.
sentences.n: رَدَيْتُ, for classical رَدَدْتُ ('I put back'), spells the doubled root as a weak one — the same leveling attested at شَقَيْتُ in Night 15. It recurs just below as اسْتَقْرَيْتُ.

sentences.t: فَخِفْتُ وَقُلْتُ السَّاعَةَ يَجِيئُونَ يُصِيبُونَ وَلَدَهُمْ مَقْتُولًا فَيَعْرِفُونَ أَنِّي قَتَلْتُهُ فَيَقْتُلُونِي لَا مَحَالَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-khiftu wa-qultu al-sāʿata yajīʾūna yuṣībūna waladahum maqtūlan fa-yaʿrifūna annī qataltuhu fa-yaqtulūnī lā maḥālata
sentences.l: So I was afraid, and I said, 'This very hour they will come; they will find their child slain; then they will know that I killed him; then they will kill me, without any doubt.'
sentences.i: I was afraid, and said to myself, 'At any moment they will come and find their child dead; they will know that I killed him, and they will surely kill me — there is no doubt of it.'
sentences.n: فَيَقْتُلُونِي keeps only one نـ where classical يَقْتُلُونَنِي (verb-ending نَ + object ـنِي) would give two in a row; a common Middle Arabic contraction, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَعَمَدْتُ إِلَى شَجَرَةٍ عَالِيَةٍ وَطَلَعْتُهَا وَاسْتَتَرْتُ بِأَوْرَاقِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿamadtu ilā shajaratin ʿāliyatin wa-ṭalaʿtuhā wa-istatartu bi-awrāqihā
sentences.l: So I made for a tall tree, and climbed it, and hid myself with its leaves.
sentences.i: So I made for a tall tree, climbed it, and hid myself among its leaves.

sentences.t: فَمَا اسْتَقْرَيْتُ فَوْقَ الشَّجَرَةِ إِلَّا وَقَدْ طَلَعَ الْعَبِيدُ وَطَلَعَ مَعَهُمُ الشَّيْخُ الْكَبِيرُ أَبُو الصَّبِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-mā istaqraytu fawqa al-shajarati illā wa-qad ṭalaʿa al-ʿabīdu wa-ṭalaʿa maʿahumu al-shaykhu al-kabīru abū al-ṣabiyyi
sentences.l: And I had hardly settled atop the tree when the slaves had already come up, and with them had come up the old man, the great one, the boy's father.
sentences.i: I had scarcely settled myself atop the tree when the slaves came up, and with them the old man, the boy's father, climbed up too.
sentences.n: اسْتَقْرَيْتُ, for classical اسْتَقْرَرْتُ ('I settled'), is the same weak-root leveling of a doubled root as رَدَيْتُ above.

sentences.t: فَجَاءُوا إِلَى الْمَوْضِعِ وَ أَزَالُوا التُّرَابَ فَوَجَدُوا الطَّابَقَ فَنَزَلُوا
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾū ilā al-mawḍiʿi wa-azālū al-turāba fa-wajadū al-ṭābaqa fa-nazalū
sentences.l: And they came to the place, and removed the earth, and found the vault, and went down.
sentences.i: They came to the spot, cleared away the earth, found the vault, and went down.
sentences.n: الطَّابَق here is the underground vault itself, as already established in Night 15, not 'floor, storey.'

sentences.t: فَوَجَدُوا الصَّبِيَّ نَائِمًا وَوَجْهُهُ يُضِيءُ مِنْ أَثَرِ الْحَمَّامِ وَهُوَ لَابِسٌ ثِيَابًا نِظَافًا وَالسِّكِّينُ مَغْرُوزَةٌ فِي صَدْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadū al-ṣabiyya nāʾiman wa-wajhuhu yuḍīʾu min athari al-ḥammāmi wa-huwa lābisun thiyāban niẓāfan wa-al-sikkīnu maghrūzatun fī ṣadrih
sentences.l: And they found the boy as if asleep, his face shining from the trace of the bath, he wearing clean garments, and the knife thrust into his breast.
sentences.i: They found the boy as though asleep, his face still glowing from the bath, dressed in clean clothes — the knife driven into his chest.

sentences.t: فَصَرَخُوا وَبَكَوْا وَلَطَمُوا عَلَى وُجُوهِهِمْ وَدَعَوْا بِالْوَيْلِ وَالثُّبُورِ وَغُشِيَ عَلَى الشَّيْخِ سَاعَةً طَوِيلَةً
sentences.tr: fa-ṣarakhū wa-bakaw wa-laṭamū ʿalā wujūhihim wa-daʿaw bi-al-wayli wa-al-thubūri wa-ghushiya ʿalā al-shaykhi sāʿatan ṭawīlatan
sentences.l: And they cried out, and wept, and struck their faces, and called out with 'Woe' and 'Perdition'; and the old man was swooned over for a long while.
sentences.i: They cried out, wept, beat their faces, and called out in woe and ruin; and the old man fell into a swoon for a long while.
sentences.n: دَعَوْا بِالْوَيْلِ وَالثُّبُورِ, 'called out with Woe and Perdition,' is the standing distress cry, a fixed pair rather than two separate calls.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعَبِيلَ ظَنُّوا أَنَّ الشَّيْخَ بَعْلَ وَلَدِهِ لَا يَعِيشُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿabīla ẓannū anna al-shaykha baʿla waladihi lā yaʿīshu
sentences.l: Then indeed the [slaves] thought that the old man, [after] his son, would not live.
sentences.i: Then the slaves thought that the old man would not survive his son.
sentences.n: Two letters here look misprinted, both ل for د: الْعَبِيل for الْعَبِيد ('the slaves,' the actors throughout this scene) and بَعْل for بَعْد ('after'), giving 'would not live after his son' — would not outlive him. Kept exactly as printed; the same ل/د slip recurs at مَلُّوا below, and again at قَلْ and بَعْلًا in the first verse.

sentences.t: وَلَفُّوا الصَّبِيَّ فِي أَثْوَابِهِ وَأَرْخَوْا عَلَيْهِ مُلَاءَةً مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ وَطَلَعُوا إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-laffū al-ṣabiyya fī athwābihi wa-arkhaw ʿalayhi mulāʾatan mina al-ḥarīri wa-ṭalaʿū ilā al-markabi
sentences.l: And they wrapped the boy in his garments, and let down over him a sheet of silk, and went up to the ship.
sentences.i: They wrapped the boy in his clothes, drew a silken sheet over him, and carried him up to the ship.

sentences.t: وَطَلَعَ الشَّيْخُ خَلْفَهُمْ فَنَظَرَ وَلَدَهُ مَمْدُودًا فَوَقَعَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṭalaʿa al-shaykhu khalfahum fa-naẓara waladahu mamdūdan fa-waqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍi
sentences.l: And the old man went up behind them, and saw his son stretched out, and he fell to the ground.
sentences.i: The old man came up behind them, and when he saw his son lying stretched out, he collapsed to the ground.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ التُّرَابَ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ وَلَطَمَ وَجْهَهُ وَنَتَفَ لِحْيَتَهُ وَتَفَكَّرَ فِي قَتْلِ وَلَدِهِ فَزَادَ بُكَاؤُهُ وَغُشِيَ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha al-turāba ʿalā raʾsihi wa-laṭama wajhahu wa-nataf liḥyatahu wa-tafakkara fī qatli waladihi fa-zāda bukāʾuhu wa-ghushiya
sentences.l: And he took the dust upon his head, and struck his face, and plucked his beard, and pondered the killing of his son; so his weeping increased, and he swooned.
sentences.i: He threw dust over his head, struck his face, tore at his beard, and brooded on his son's murder; his weeping grew, and he fell again into a swoon.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعَ عَبْدٌ مِنْهُمْ فَجَاءَ بِمَقْطَعِ حَرِيرٍ وَمَلُّوا الشَّيْخَ عَلَى الْمَقْعَدِ وَجَلَسُوا عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿa ʿabdun minhum fa-jāʾa bi-maqṭaʿi ḥarīrin wa-mallū al-shaykha ʿalā al-maqʿadi wa-jalasū ʿinda raʾsihi
sentences.l: Then a slave among them went up, and brought a length of silk, and they [mallū] the old man onto the couch, and sat by his head.
sentences.i: Then one of the slaves went up and brought a piece of silk; they laid the old man out on the couch and sat by his head.
sentences.n: مَلُّوا has no sense of its own here ('grew weary of'); most likely another ل for د, for مَدُّوا 'they stretched him out' — the third instance of this letter-slip in the passage (see the note two units above). Translated by that sense; the letters are kept exactly as printed.

sentences.t: هَذَا كُلُّهُ وَأَنَا فِى الشَّجَرَةِ فَوْقَ رُؤْسِهِمْ أَنْظُرُ مَا يَجْرِى
sentences.tr: hādhā kulluhu wa-anā fī al-shajarati fawqa ruʾsihim anẓuru mā yajrī
sentences.l: All this while I was in the tree, above their heads, watching what was happening.
sentences.i: All this while, I was up in the tree above their heads, watching everything that happened.
sentences.n: فى and يجرى keep the archive's alif-maqsūra spelling of fī and yajrī. رُؤْسِهِمْ — one wāw short of the full plural رُؤُوس 'heads' — is the identical defective spelling already met and flagged in Night 15's own occurrence of this word; kept the same way here.

sentences.t: وَقَلْ شَابَ قَلْبِي قَبْلَ أَنْ يَشِيبَ رَأْسِي بِمَا قَاسَيْتُ مِنَ الْهُمُومِ وَالْأَحْزَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad shāba qalbī qabla an yashība raʾsī bimā qāsaytu mina al-humūmi wa-al-aḥzāni
sentences.l: And [indeed] my heart had gone grey before my head grew grey, from what I had suffered of cares and sorrows.
sentences.i: My heart had turned grey before my head did, from all the grief and sorrow I had endured.
sentences.n: قَلْ has no sense of its own here; almost certainly a fourth instance of the ل/د slip already noted twice above, for قَدْ ('indeed'), giving the natural 'my heart had already gone grey before my head did.' Kept exactly as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَدْتُ أَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-anshadtu aqūlu
sentences.l: And I recited, saying:
sentences.i: And I recited these lines:

sentences.t:
وَكَمْ لِلَّهِ مِنْ لُطْفٍ خَفِيٍّ * يَدِقُّ خَفَاهُ عَنْ فَهْمِ الذَّكِى
وَكَمْ أَمْرٍ تُسَاءُ بِهِ صَبَاحًا * فَتَأْتِيكَ الْمَسَرَّةُ بِالْعَشِى
وَكَمْ يُسْرٍأَتَي مِنْ بَعْلِ عُسْرٍ * فَفَرَّجَ كُرْبَةَ الْقَلْبِ الشَّجِى
sentences.tr:
wa-kam li-llāhi min luṭfin khafiyyin * yadiqqu khafāhu ʿan fahmi al-dhakī
wa-kam amrin tusāʾu bihi ṣabāḥan * fa-taʾtīka al-masarratu bi-al-ʿashī
wa-kam yusrin atā min baʿdi ʿusrin * fa-farraja kurbata al-qalbi al-shajī
sentences.l:
And how many a hidden kindness belongs to God * whose hiddenness eludes the understanding of the clever!
And how many a matter grieves you in the morning * yet gladness comes to you by evening!
And how much ease has come after hardship * and so relieved the anguish of the grieving heart!
sentences.i: How many a mercy from God lies hidden, too fine for even a keen mind to grasp! How often a thing that grieves you at dawn is followed by joy that reaches you by dusk! How often ease arrives on the heels of hardship, and lifts the sorrow from a grieving heart!
sentences.n: بَعْلِ is read as بَعْدِ 'after' — the same ل/د slip noted twice already. يُسْرٍأَتَى ('an ease came') is printed as one unbroken run with no word-space; the two words are read continuously without adding, removing, or changing a letter.

sentences.t: يَا سَيِّدَتِي وَلَمْ يَزَلِ الشَّيْخُ فِي غَشْوَتِهِ إِلَى أَنْ قَرُبَ الْمَغْرِبُ
sentences.tr: yā sayyidatī wa-lam yazali al-shaykhu fī ghashwatihi ilā an qaruba al-maghribu
sentences.l: O my lady, the old man did not cease [being] in his swoon until sunset drew near.
sentences.i: O my lady, the old man remained in his swoon until sunset drew near.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اسْتَفَاقَ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى وَلَدِهِ وَمَا جَرَى لَهُ وَالَّذِي خَافَ مِنْهُ وَقَعَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma istafāqa wa-naẓara ilā waladihi wa-mā jarā lahu wa-al-ladhī khāfa minhu waqaʿa fīhi
sentences.l: Then he awoke, and looked at his son and what had happened to him; and that which he had feared had befallen him.
sentences.i: Then he came to himself, and looked at his son and all that had befallen him; the very thing he had dreaded had come to pass.

sentences.t: وَ لَطَمَ وَجْهَهُ وَرَأْسَهُ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-laṭama wajhahu wa-raʾsahu wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And he struck his face and his head, and recited these verses:
sentences.i: And he struck his face and his head, and recited these verses:

sentences.t:
الْقَلْبُ مِنْ فُرْقَةِ الْأَحْبَابِ مُنْصَدِعٌ * أَمَّا دُمُوعِي مِنَ الْآمَاقِ تَنْهَمِلُ
شَطَّ الْمَرَامُ بِهِمْ بَعْلًا فَوَا أَسَفِي * مَا حِيلَتِي فِيهِمْ مَا الْقَوْلُ مَا الْعَمَلُ
فَلَيْتَنِي مَا كُنْتُ نَظَرْتُهُمْ أَبَدًا * مَا حِيلَتِي سَادَتِي ضَاقَتْ بِى السُّبُلُ
كَيْفَ السُّلُوُّ بِسُلْوَانٍ وَقَدْ لَعِبَتْ * نَارُ الْهَوَى بِعَوَادِي وَهِيَ تَشْتَعِلُ
يَا لَيْتَ لَوْ يَمَّمَتْ ذَاتَ الْمَنُونِ بِهِمْ * بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُمْ مَا لَيْسَ يَنْفَصِلُ
سَأَلْتُكَ اللَّهَ يَا وَاشِي فَكُنْ مَهْلًا * فَجَمْعُ شَمْلِي بِهِمْ مَازَالَ مُشْتَمِلُ
مَا كَانَ أَحْسَنَنَا وَالدَّارُ تَجْمَعُنَا * وَنَحْنُ فِي غِبْطَةٍ وَالْعَيْشُ مُتَّصِلُ
حَتَّى رُمِينَا بِسَهْمِ الْبَيْنِ فَرَّقَنَا * مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي لِسِهَامِ الْبَيْنِ يَحْتَمِلُ
إِذْ صَابَنَا فِي عَزِيزِ الْقَوْمِ عَائِبَةٌ * فَرِيدِ عَصْرٍ غَدَا بِالْحُسْنِ مُكْتَمِلُ
أَنْشَدْتُهُ وَلِسَانُ الْحَالِ يَسْبِقُنِي * يَا لَيْتَ يَا وَلَدِي مَا قَدْ أَتَى الْأَجَلُ
كَيْفَ السَّبِيلُ إِلَى لُقْيَاكُمْ عَجِّلْ * نَفْدِيكَ يَا وَلَدِي بِالرُّوحِ لَوْ قُبِلْ
إِنْ قُلْتُ شَمْسٌ فَإِنَّ الشَّمْسَ غَارِبَةٌ * أَوْ قُلْتُ بَدْرٌ فَإِنَّ الْبَدْرَ قَدْ أَفَلْ
لَهْفِي عَلَيْكَ مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ يَا أَسَفِي * مَا عَنْكَ بُدَّ فَمَنْ ذَا عَنْكَ يَشْتَغِلُ
أَبُوكَ أَضْحَى بِهِ شَوْقًا إِلَيْكَ وَمَا * حَلَّ الْمَمَاتُ بِكُمْ ضَاقَتْ بِيَ الْحِيَلُ
عَيْنُ الْحَوَاسِدِ فِينَا الْيَوْمَ قَدْ وَقَعَتْ * يَلْقَوْنَ مَا صَنَعُوا يَا بِئْسَ مَا فَعَلُوا
sentences.tr:
al-qalbu min furqati al-aḥbābi munṣadiʿun * ammā dumūʿī mina al-āmāqi tanhamilu
shaṭṭa al-marāmu bihim baʿlan fa-wā asafī * mā ḥīlatī fīhim mā al-qawlu mā al-ʿamalu
fa-laytanī mā kuntu naẓartuhum abadan * mā ḥīlatī sādatī ḍāqat biya al-subulu
kayfa al-sulūwu bi-sulwānin wa-qad laʿibat * nāru al-hawā bi-ʿawādī wa-hiya tashtaʿilu
yā layta law yammamat dhāta al-manūni bihim * baynī wa-baynahum mā laysa yanfaṣilu
saʾaltuka Allāha yā wāshī fa-kun mahlan * fa-jamʿu shamlī bihim mā zāla mushtamilu
mā kāna aḥsananā wa-al-dāru tajmaʿunā * wa-naḥnu fī ghibṭatin wa-al-ʿayshu muttaṣilu
ḥattā rumīnā bi-sahmi al-bayni farraqanā * man dhā al-ladhī li-sihāmi al-bayni yaḥtamilu
idh ṣābanā fī ʿazīzi al-qawmi ʿāʾibatun * farīdi ʿaṣrin ghadā bi-al-ḥusni muktamilu
anshadtuhu wa-lisānu al-ḥāli yasbiqunī * yā layta yā waladī mā qad atā al-ajalu
kayfa al-sabīlu ilā luqyākum ʿajjil * nafdīka yā waladī bi-al-rūḥi law qubil
in qultu shamsun fa-inna al-shamsa ghāribatun * aw qultu badrun fa-inna al-badra qad afal
lahfī ʿalayka mina al-ayyāmi yā asafī * mā ʿanka budda fa-man dhā ʿanka yashtaghilu
abūka aḍḥā bihi shawqan ilayka wa-mā * ḥalla al-mamātu bikum ḍāqat biya al-ḥiyalu
ʿaynu al-ḥawāsidi fīnā al-yawma qad waqaʿat * yalqawna mā ṣanaʿū yā biʾsa mā faʿalū
sentences.l:
The heart, from the parting of the loved-ones, is riven * as for my tears, from the eyes' corners they pour down.
The desired-thing has grown remote regarding them, far off — oh, alas for my grief! * What is my recourse concerning them? What is the saying, what is the deed?
Would that I had never looked upon them at all! * What is my recourse, my masters — the ways have grown strait for me.
How is forgetting, by any consolation, when the fire of passion has played through my very being * and it blazes?
Would that, though the mistress of doom had made straight for them * there yet remained between me and them what does not sever!
I ask you, by God, O tale-bearer, be gentle * for the gathering of my scattered-state with them has never ceased to hold entire.
How good we were, while the house gathered us * and we in gladness, and the life unbroken!
Until we were struck by the arrow of separation, [which] parted us * who is there that can bear the arrows of separation?
When a fault/calamity befell us in the dear-one of the folk * the unique-one of an age, grown perfect in beauty.
I recited it to him, while the tongue-of-the-state outran me: * 'Would, O my son, that the appointed-term had not come!'
How is the way to meeting-you? Make haste! * We would ransom you, O my son, with the soul, were it accepted.
If I say 'a sun,' then indeed the sun sets * or if I say 'a full-moon,' then indeed the full-moon has already gone down.
My grief for you, from the days — oh my sorrow! * There is no escape from you; so who is it that can turn away from you?
Your father has become, in this, full of longing for you * and since death has alighted upon you, [my] resources have grown strait for me.
The eye of the enviers has fallen upon us this day * let them meet what they have done — evil is what they have done!
sentences.i: My heart is riven by the parting of those I love; as for my tears, they stream down from the corners of my eyes. My hope of them has grown distant, far away — ah, the grief of it! What recourse have I in their case? What is there to say, what is there to do? Would that I had never set eyes on them at all! What can I do, my dear ones — every path has closed in on me. How can consolation ever bring forgetfulness, when the fire of love has played through my very heart, and still burns on? Would that, though Doom herself had claimed them, there still remained between us a bond that could never be severed! I beg you, by God, O tale-bearer, be gentle — for my bond with them has never ceased to hold entire. How fair we were, when one roof still gathered us together, and we lived on in gladness, our days flowing unbroken! Until the arrow of parting struck us and drove us apart; who is there that can withstand the arrows of separation? When calamity struck us in the person of our precious one — that peerless one of his age, grown perfect in beauty. I recited this to him, while the voice of my very condition outran my words: 'Would, O my son, that your hour had never come!' Is there any way to reach you? Make haste! We would give our very souls to ransom you, my son, if only it could be accepted! If I call you a sun, the sun still sets; if I call you a full moon, the full moon still wanes and is gone. How I grieve for you because of these days — ah, my sorrow! There is no escaping your loss; who could ever turn his mind from you? Your father has become consumed with longing for you; and since death has taken you, every resource within me has failed. The eye of the envious has fallen upon us this day; let them meet the reward of what they have done — evil indeed is what they have done!
sentences.n: بَعْلًا (l.2) again reads as بَعْدًا 'far off' — the same ل/د slip noted several times already in this passage. عَجِّلْ (l.11) is read as the imperative 'make haste,' the one line here printed with no accusative-tanwīn alif at all. بِعَوَادِي (l.4) is obscure — perhaps 'my inmost being' or 'my wonted state' — and is rendered loosely; vocalized as printed rather than emended. All fifteen lines carry one continuous monorhyme in -l (rawī lām), confirming they belong to a single unbroken recitation.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَهَقَ شَهْقَةً فَارَقَتْ رُوحُهُ جَسَدَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma shahaqa shahqatan fāraqat rūḥuhu jasadahu
sentences.l: Then he gasped a gasp, [and] his soul parted from his body.
sentences.i: Then he gave a single gasp, and his soul left his body.

sentences.t: فَصَرَخُوا الْعَبِيدُ وَا سَيِّدَاهْ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣarakhū al-ʿabīdu wā sayyidāh
sentences.l: And the slaves cried out, ‘Alas, master!’
sentences.i: And the slaves cried out, ‘Alas, our master!’
sentences.n: الْعَبِيدُ, though it follows the verb, is its subject; the verb still carries the plural ending, as noted earlier in the frame story (“the fleas ate me” agreement). سَيِّدَاهْ names their master — apparently the jeweller who has just descended to leave his son hidden in the vault and has died on the spot, seemingly of grief; وَا + noun + the lengthened -اه is the fixed cry of lament.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذُوا التُّرَابَ عَلَى رُؤُسِهِمْ وَزَادُوا فِى الْبُكَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhū al-turāba ʿalā ruʾusihim wa-zādū fī al-bukāʾi
sentences.l: and they took the dust upon their heads and increased in the weeping,
sentences.i: and they threw dust upon their heads and wept the more,
sentences.n: رُؤُسِهِمْ is spelled defectively for classical رُؤُوسِهِمْ — the plural's second wāw is not written, exactly as قل elsewhere stands for قال — and is pointed here as the print gives it.

sentences.t: وَطَلَعُوا لِسَيِّدِهِمْ فِى الْمَرْكَبِ إِلَى جَانِبِ وَلَدِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṭalaʿū li-sayyidihim fī al-markabi ilā jānibi waladihi
sentences.l: and they went up, [bringing] their master, into the ship, to the side of his son,
sentences.i: and they carried their master up into the ship and laid him beside his son,
sentences.n: “His son” here is apparently a second son of the jeweller who had stayed aboard the ship, distinct from the boy left hidden below.

sentences.t: وَأَرْخَوْا قِلْعَ الْمَرْكَبِ فَغَابُوا عَنْ عَيْنِي
sentences.tr: wa-arkhaw qilʿa al-markabi fa-ghābū ʿan ʿaynī
sentences.l: and they slackened the ship's sail, and they vanished from my eye,
sentences.i: and they let down the ship's sail and passed out of my sight,

sentences.t: فَنَزَلْتُ مِنْ فَوْقِ الشَّجَرَةِ وَنَزَلْتُ الطَّابِقَ
sentences.tr: fa-nazaltu min fawqi al-shajarati wa-nazaltu al-ṭābiqa
sentences.l: and I came down from atop the tree, and I went down [into] the vault,
sentences.i: so I climbed down from the tree and went down into the vault,
sentences.n: الطَّابِقَ takes a bare accusative where نزل classically governs إلى — the same direct-transitive habit as قَرُبَ مَدِينَتَهُ in the frame story; it recurs several times below (أَنْزِلُ الْقَاعَةَ, تَفَكَّرْتُ الشَّابَّ, أَطْلَعُونِي الْقَصْرَ).

sentences.t: وَتَفَكَّرْتُ الشَّابَّ فَرَأَيْتُ بَعْضَ حَوَائِجَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-tafakkartu al-shābba fa-raʾaytu baʿḍa ḥawāʾijahu
sentences.l: and I thought upon the youth, and I saw some of his belongings,
sentences.i: and I fell to thinking of the young man, and caught sight of some of his things,

sentences.t: فَأَنْشَدْتُ أَقُولُ شِعْرًا
sentences.tr: fa-anshadtu aqūlu shiʿran
sentences.l: and I recited — I say verse:
sentences.i: and I recited these verses:
sentences.n: أَنْشَدْتُ أَقُولُ شِعْرًا is the fixed formula introducing a poem throughout the Nights; أَقُولُ شِعْرًا adds nothing beyond “reciting” and can simply be read as “saying.”

sentences.t:
أَرَى آثَارَهُمْ فَأَذُوبُ شَوْقًا * وَأَسْكُبُ فِي مَوَاطِنِهِمْ دُمُوعِي
وَأَسْأَلُ مَنْ قَضَى بِالْبُعْدِ عَنْهُمْ * يَمُنَّ عَلَيَّ يَوْمًا بِالرُّجُوعِ
sentences.tr:
arā āthārahum fa-adhūbu shawqan * wa-askubu fī mawāṭinihim dumūʿī
wa-asʾalu man qaḍā bi-al-buʿdi ʿanhum * yamunna ʿalayya yawman bi-al-rujūʿ
sentences.l:
I see their traces, and I melt with longing * and I pour, in their dwelling-places, my tears.
And I ask Him who decreed [our] separation from them * that He grant me, one day, the return.
sentences.i:
I look upon the traces they have left, and melt with longing; I pour out my tears where they once dwelt.
And I pray to Him who ordained our parting from them that He grant me, one day, to come back.
sentences.n: An implied أَنْ governs يَمُنَّ (subjunctive) after أَسْأَلُ, elided under poetic license; بِـ after يَمُنَّ عَلَى marks what is bestowed (‘grant X’), just as بِالْبُعْدِ marks what قَضَى decreed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي يَا سَيِّدَتِي خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الطَّابِقِ
sentences.tr: thumma innī yā sayyidatī kharajtu mina al-ṭābiqi
sentences.l: Then, indeed I — O my lady — went out from the vault,
sentences.i: Then, O my lady, I came up out of the vault,

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ بِالنَّهَارِ الطَّوْفَ فِى الْجَزِيرَةِ وَبِاللَّيْلِ أَنْزِلُ الْقَاعَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu bi-al-nahāri al-ṭawfa fī al-jazīrati wa-bi-al-layli anzilu al-qāʿata
sentences.l: and I was, by day, the roaming in the island, and by night I go down [into] the hall,
sentences.i: and by day I would wander about the island, and by night go down into the underground hall,
sentences.n: كُنْتُ...الطَّوْفَ makes the verbal noun itself the predicate of كان rather than following it with an imperfect verb — a habitual ‘I was a-roaming’; the second half continues the same habitual sense with a plain imperfect, أَنْزِلُ.

sentences.t: فَأَقَمْتُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ شَهْرًا وَأَنَا أَنْظُرُ إِلَى طَرَفِ الْجَزِيرَةِ الَّتِي مِنْ نَاحِيَةِ الْغَرْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-aqamtu ʿalā dhālika shahran wa-anā anẓuru ilā ṭarafi al-jazīrati allatī min nāḥiyati al-gharbi
sentences.l: and I remained upon that a month, while I [was] looking toward the edge of the island which is on the side of the west,
sentences.i: and I stayed thus a month, watching the edge of the island that lay to the west,

sentences.t: وَهُوَ كُلَّ مَا مَرَّ يَوْمٌ مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ يَنْشَفُ الْبَحْرُ إِلَى أَنْ قَلَّ الْمَاءُ مِنْ جِهَةِ الْغَرْبِ وَانْقَطَعَ تَيَّارُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa kulla mā marra yawmun mina al-ayyāmi yanshafu al-baḥru ilā an qalla al-māʾu min jihati al-gharbi wa-inqaṭaʿa tayyāruhu
sentences.l: and it [was]: every [time] a day of the days passed, the sea would dry up, until the water lessened from the direction of the west and its current was cut off,
sentences.i: for every day that passed, the sea would dry back a little, until the water had shrunk away on the western side and its current failed,
sentences.n: كُلَّ مَا is printed as two words (elsewhere fused as كُلَّمَا, ‘whenever’); the sense is unaffected.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَمَلَ الشَّهْرُ نَشَفَ الْبَحْرُ مِنْ تِلْكَ النَّاحِيَةِ فَفَرِحْتُ وَأَيْقَنْتُ بِالسَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kamala al-shahru nashafa al-baḥru min tilka al-nāḥiyati fa-fariḥtu wa-ayqantu bi-al-salāmati
sentences.l: And when the month was complete, the sea dried up from that side, and I rejoiced and became certain of the safety,
sentences.i: And when the month was complete, the sea had dried away on that side, so I rejoiced and felt sure of my safety,

sentences.t: وَ قُمْتُ خُضْتُ مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ الْبَحْرِ وَ طَلَعْتُ إِلَى الْبَرِّ الْأَصِيلِ
sentences.tr: wa-qumtu khuḍtu mā baqiya mina al-baḥri wa-ṭalaʿtu ilā al-barri al-aṣīli
sentences.l: and I rose, I waded [through] what remained of the sea, and I came out onto the firm mainland,
sentences.i: and I rose up, waded through what was left of the sea, and came out onto solid ground,

sentences.t: فَلَقِيتُ كِيمَانَ رَمْلٍ تَغُوصُ رِجْلُ الْجَمَلِ فِيهَا إِلَى الرُّكَبِ فَقَوِيَتْ رُوحِي
sentences.tr: fa-laqītu kīmāna ramlin taghūṣu rijlu al-jamali fīhā ilā al-rukabi fa-qawiyat rūḥī
sentences.l: and I came upon mounds of sand in which the foot of the camel sinks up to the knees, and my spirit grew strong,
sentences.i: and I came upon dunes of sand, deep enough to swallow a camel's foot to the knee, and my spirits rose,
sentences.n: الرُّكَبِ, ‘the knees,’ is the plural of رُكْبَة without its تاء — the ordinary plural of this pattern (كَلِمَة / كَلِم), not a defective spelling.

sentences.t: وَ قَطَعْتُ الرَّمْلَ وَ إِذَا أَنَا بِنَارٍ تَلُوحُ مِنْ بَعِيدٍ وَهِيَ تَشْتَعِلُ اشْتِعَالًا قَوِيًّا
sentences.tr: wa-qaṭaʿtu al-ramla wa-idhā anā bi-nārin talūḥu min baʿīdin wa-hiya tashtaʿilu ishtiʿālan qawiyyan
sentences.l: and I crossed the sand, and behold, I [was] with a fire gleaming from afar, and it [was] blazing a mighty blazing,
sentences.i: and I made my way across the sand, and suddenly there was a fire glimmering in the distance, blazing fiercely,
sentences.n: وَإِذَا أَنَا بِـ is the إِذَا of surprise, ‘and there I was, faced with…’; the بِـ marks what appears, exactly as in وَإِذَا بِغَزَالَةٍ, ‘and behold, a gazelle.’

sentences.t: فَقَصَدْتُهَا لَعَلِّي أَجِلُ فَرَجًا وَ أَنْشَدْتُ أَقُولُ شِعْرًا
sentences.tr: fa-qaṣadtuhā laʿallī ajilu farajan wa-anshadtu aqūlu shiʿran
sentences.l: so I made for it, that perhaps I might — find(?) — relief, and I recited, I say verse:
sentences.i: so I made toward it, hoping I might find some relief, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: أَجِلُ is obscure: the sense plainly wants ‘I may find/attain’ (perhaps أَجِدُ, dāl and lām being easily confused in this print); pointed here as printed, on the pattern of the verb it most likely stands for.

sentences.t:
عَسَى وَ لَعَلَّ الدَّهْرَ يَلْوِي عِنَانَهُ * وَ يَأْتِي بِخَيْرٍ وَ الزَّمَانُ غَيُورٌ
وَ يَسْعِفُ آمَالِي وَ يَقْضِي حَوَائِجِي * وَ تُحْدِثُ مِنْ بَعْدِ الْأُمُورِ أُمُورٌ
sentences.tr:
ʿasā wa-laʿalla al-dahra yalwī ʿinānahu * wa-yaʾatī bi-khayrin wa-al-zamānu ghayūrun
wa-yasʿifu āmālī wa-yaqḍī ḥawāʾijī * wa-tuḥdithu min baʿdi al-umūri umūrun
sentences.l:
Perhaps — and it may be — that fate will turn its rein * and bring good, though time is jealous
and [that it] will further my hopes and fulfil my needs * for after [certain] matters, [other] matters come to be.
sentences.i: Perhaps fate will yet turn its rein and bring good, jealous though time can be; perhaps it will speed my hopes and grant my wishes — for one thing follows upon another.
sentences.n: وَتُحْدِثُ مِنْ بَعْدِ الْأُمُورِ أُمُورٌ is proverbial: ‘matters bring forth [further] matters after [earlier] matters’ — one thing leads to another.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي قَصَدْتُ النَّارَ فَلَمَّا قَرُبْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَ إِذَا بِقَصْرٍ بَابُهُ مِنَ النُّحَاسِ الْأَصْفَرِ
sentences.tr: thumma innī qaṣadtu al-nāra fa-lammā qarubtu ilayhā wa-idhā bi-qaṣrin bābuhu mina al-nuḥāsi al-aṣfari
sentences.l: Then, indeed I made for the fire; and when I drew near to it, behold, [there was] a palace, its door of the yellow brass,
sentences.i: So I made for the fire, and when I drew near it, there before me was a palace whose door was of yellow brass,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَشْرَقَتْ عَلَيْهِ الشَّمْسُ أَضَاءَ مِنْ بَعِيدٍ يُرَى كَأَنَّهُ نَارٌ فَفَرِحْتُ بِرُؤْيَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ashraqat ʿalayhi al-shamsu aḍāʾa min baʿīdin yurā kaʾannahu nārun fa-fariḥtu bi-ruʾyatihi
sentences.l: and when the sun shone upon it, it gleamed from afar — it is seen as though it [were] a fire — and I rejoiced at the sight of it,
sentences.i: and when the sun struck it, it shone from a distance so that it looked just like fire, and I rejoiced at the sight of it,

sentences.t: وَ جَلَسْتُ مُقَابِلًا بَابَهُ فَلَمْ يَسْتَقِرَّ لِي الْجُلُوسُ حَتَّى أَقْبَلَ عَشَرَةُ شَبَابٍ لَابِسِينَ الْأَثْوَابَ الْمُفْتَخِرَةَ وَ مَعَهُمْ شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-jalastu muqābilan bābahu fa-lam yastaqirra lī al-julūsu ḥattā aqbala ʿasharatu shabābin lābisīna al-athwāba al-muftakhirata wa-maʿahum shaykhun kabīrun
sentences.l: and I sat facing its door; and the sitting had not settled for me before ten young men came forward, wearing the splendid garments, and with them an old shaykh,
sentences.i: and I sat down facing its door; and I had scarcely settled myself when ten young men came up, dressed in magnificent robes, with an old shaykh among them—

sentences.t: إِلَّا أَنَّ الشَّبَابَ عُورٌ بِالْعَيْنِ الْيُمْنَى
sentences.tr: illā anna al-shabāba ʿūrun bi-al-ʿayni al-yumnā
sentences.l: except that the young men [were] one-eyed in the right eye.
sentences.i: except that the young men were blind in the right eye.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبْتُ بِصِفَتِهِمْ وَ إِنْفَاقِهِمْ فِي عَوَرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabtu bi-ṣifatihim wa-infāqihim fī ʿawarihim
sentences.l: and I marveled at their appearance and their spending, in their one-eyedness,
sentences.i: and I marveled at their fine looks and their evident wealth, disfigured as they were,
sentences.n: إِنْفَاقُهُمْ, ‘their spending,’ is the plain sense of the print — their outlay on such splendid dress, remarkable given that the loss of an eye was no mark of fortune; فِي here carries the concessive force ‘despite,’ not merely ‘in.’

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْنِي سَلَّمُوا عَلَيَّ وَ سَأَلُونِي عَنْ حَالِي وَ قِصَّتِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawnī sallamū ʿalayya wa-saʾalūnī ʿan ḥālī wa-qiṣṣatī
sentences.l: and when they saw me, they greeted upon me, and they asked me about my condition and my story,
sentences.i: and when they saw me, they greeted me and asked after my condition and my story,

sentences.t: فَحَكَيْتُ لَهُمْ عَلَى مَا جَرَى لِي وَ مَا تَمَّ لِي مِنَ الْمَصَائِبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥakaytu lahum ʿalā mā jarā lī wa-mā tamma lī mina al-maṣāʾibi
sentences.l: and I related to them concerning what had happened to me and what had come to pass for me of the calamities,
sentences.i: and I told them all that had happened to me and the misfortunes that had befallen me,

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبُوا لِحَدِيثِي وَ أَخَذُونِي وَ أَطْلَعُونِي الْقَصْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabū li-ḥadīthī wa-akhadhūnī wa-aṭlaʿūnī al-qaṣra
sentences.l: and they marveled at my account, and they took me and brought me up [into] the palace,
sentences.i: and they marveled at my story, and took me and brought me up into the palace,
sentences.n: أَطْلَعُونِي الْقَصْرَ, like أَنْزِلُ الْقَاعَةَ and نَزَلْتُ الطَّابِقَ above, drops the preposition (عَلَى) the verb would classically take.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ فِي دَائِرِ الْقَصْرِ عَشَرَةَ تُخُوتٍ وَ كُلُّ تَخْتٍ فِرَاشُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu fī dāʾiri al-qaṣri ʿasharata tukhūtin wa-kullu takhtin firāshuhu
sentences.l: and I saw, around the palace, ten couches, and each couch, its mattress
sentences.i: and I saw, ranged about the palace, ten couches, each with its mattress

sentences.t: وَ لِحَافُهُ أَزْرَقُ وَ فِي وَسَطِ تِلْكَ التُّخُوتِ تَخْتٌ صَغِيرٌ وَ هُوَ مِثْلُهُمْ كُلِّهِمْ عَلَيْهِ أَزْرَقُ
sentences.tr: wa-liḥāfuhu azraqu wa-fī wasaṭi tilka al-tukhūti takhtun ṣaghīrun wa-huwa mithluhum kullihim ʿalayhi azraqu
sentences.l: and its coverlet, blue; and in the middle of those couches [was] a small couch, and it [was] like all of them — blue upon it,
sentences.i: and its coverlet, both blue; and in the middle of them stood a small couch, furnished in blue like all the rest,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلْنَا طَلَعَ كُلُّ شَابٍّ عَلَى تَخْتِهِ وَ طَلَعَ الشَّيْخُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ التَّخْتِ الصَّغِيرِ الَّذِي فِي وَسَطِ التُّخُوتِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhalnā ṭalaʿa kullu shābbin ʿalā takhtihi wa-ṭalaʿa al-shaykhu ʿalā dhālika al-takhti al-ṣaghīri alladhī fī wasaṭi al-tukhūti
sentences.l: and when we entered, each young man mounted his couch, and the shaykh mounted that small couch which [was] in the middle of the couches,
sentences.i: and when we went in, each young man took his own couch, and the shaykh took the small couch in their midst,

sentences.t: وَ قَالَ يَا فَتَى اجْلِسْ فِي هَذَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā fatā ijlis fī hādhā
sentences.l: and he said, ‘O young man, sit in this —’
sentences.i: and he said, ‘Sit down here, young man —’
sentences.n: The shaykh's speech breaks off here, mid-sentence, and continues in what follows.

sentences.t: الْقَصْرَ وَ لَا تَسْأَلْ عَنْ أَحْوَالِنَا وَ لَا عَنْ عَوَرِ أَعْيُيْنِنَا
sentences.tr: al-qaṣra wa-lā tasʾal ʿan aḥwālinā wa-lā ʿan ʿawari aʿyuyninā
sentences.l: — the palace, and do not ask about our conditions, nor about the one-eyedness of our eyes —
sentences.i: — the palace, and ask nothing about our lives, or about the blindness in our eyes —
sentences.n: This opens mid-sentence: the object "the palace" and the command before it belong to speech begun earlier (the young men inviting the qalandar in). The archive spells "our eyes" أعيينِنا with an extra ي beyond the expected أَعْيُنِنَا; kept as printed, vocalized with the extra letter silent.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ الشَّيْخُ وَ قَدَّمَ لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ طَعَامًا فِي إِنَاءٍ وَ شَرَابًا فِي إِنَاءٍ وَ قَدَّمَ لِي كَذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma al-shaykhu wa-qaddama li-kulli wāḥidin ṭaʿāman fī ināʾin wa-sharāban fī ināʾin wa-qaddama lī kadhālika
sentences.l: Then the old man rose, and set before each one food in a vessel and drink in a vessel, and set before me likewise.

sentences.t: وَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ جَلَسُوا يَسْأَلُونِي عَنْ أَحْوَالِي وَ مَا جَرِئَ لِي وَ أَنَا أُخْبِرُهُمْ إِلَى أَنْ ذَهَبَ أَكْثَرُ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika jalasū yasʾalūnī ʿan aḥwālī wa-mā jariʾa lī wa-anā ukhbiruhum ilā an dhahaba aktharu al-layli
sentences.l: And after that they sat questioning me about my condition and what had happened to me, and I would tell them, until most of the night had gone.
sentences.n: جَرِئَ (for the expected جَرَى, "happened") is spelled here with a hamza-seat ئ; the same word recurs at P114L09 spelled ordinarily, جرى. Both kept as printed, not harmonized.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشَّبَابُ أَيُّهَا الشَّيْخُ مَا تُقَدِّمُ لَنَا رَاتِبَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shabābu ayyuhā al-shaykhu mā tuqaddimu lanā rātibanā
sentences.l: Then the young men said, "O old man, will you not bring us our ration?"

sentences.t: فَقٰلَ جَاءَ وَقْتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla jāʾa waqtuhu
sentences.l: And he said, "Its time has come."
sentences.n: قٰل (for قال) is the edition's own defective spelling, pointed here with the dagger alif. No speaker is named; by the parallel exchange later in this passage ("هات لنا راتبنا" / "قل جاء وقت النوم", both unambiguously the old man's words), this is most likely the old man confirming, not the young men repeating their request.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: And he said, "Gladly and with honor."
sentences.i: And he said, "Of course — gladly!"
sentences.n: The speaker of this short interjection is likewise unmarked; taken here as the old man's agreement, though it could belong to the young men instead.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ وَ دَخَلَ إِلَى مَخْدَعٍ فِي الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma wa-dakhala ilā makhdaʿin fī al-qaṣri
sentences.l: Then he rose and went into a chamber in the palace.

sentences.t: وَغَابَ وَعَادَ وَعَلَى رَأْسِهِ عَشَرَةُ أَطْبَاقٍ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مُغَطًّى بِغِطَاءٍ أَزْرَقَ
sentences.tr: wa-ghāba wa-ʿāda wa-ʿalā raʾsihi ʿasharatu aṭbāqin kullu wāḥidin mughaṭṭan bi-ghiṭāʾin azraqa
sentences.l: And he disappeared and came back, and upon his head [were] ten trays, each one covered with a blue cover.

sentences.t: فَقَدَّمَ لِكُلِّ شَابٍّ طَبَقًا ثُمَّ أَوْقَدَ عَشَرَةَ شُمُوعٍ وَأَغْرَزَ عَلَى كُلِّ طَبَقٍ شَمْعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qaddama li-kulli shābbin ṭabaqan thumma awqada ʿasharata shumūʿin wa-aghraza ʿalā kulli ṭabaqin shamʿatan
sentences.l: Then he set before each young man a tray, then lit ten candles, and planted a candle upon each tray.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَشَفَ الْأَغْطِيَةَ فَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهَا فِى الْأَطْبَاقِ رَمَادٌ وَدَقُّ فَحْمٍ وَسَوَادُ الْقَلْبِ
sentences.tr: thumma kashafa al-aghṭiyata fa-bāna min taḥtihā fī al-aṭbāqi ramādun wa-daqqu faḥmin wa-sawādu al-qalbi
sentences.l: Then he lifted the covers, and there appeared from beneath them, in the trays, ash, and crushed charcoal, and the black of the wick.
sentences.n: قَلْب is taken here in its attested sense "wick" (of a lamp), giving "lamp-black, soot" — not "heart" — which fits a list of blackening agents; the more obvious reading "blackness of the heart" does not suit the context.

sentences.t: فَشَمَّرَ الْجَمِيعُ عَنْ سَوَاعِدِهِمْ وَبَكَوْا وَانْتَحَبُوا وَسَخَّمُوا وُجُوهَهُمْ وَ خَبَطُوا أَثْوَابَهُمْ وَلَطَمُوا عَلَى وُجُوهِهِمْ وَدَقُّوا عَلَى صُدُورِهِمْ وَعَارُوا يَقُولُونَ كُنَّا قَاعِدِينَ بِطُولِنَا مَا خَلَّانَا فُضُولُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-shammara al-jamīʿu ʿan sawāʿidihim wa-bakaw wa-intaḥabū wa-sakhkhamū wujūhahum wa-khabaṭū athwābahum wa-laṭamū ʿalā wujūhihim wa-daqqū ʿalā ṣudūrihim wa-ʿārū yaqūlūna kunnā qāʿidīna bi-ṭūlinā mā khallānā fuḍūlunā
sentences.l: Then all of them rolled up their sleeves and wept and sobbed and blackened their faces and beat their garments and struck their faces and pounded their chests and were seized with shame, saying: "We sat at our ease — our own prying would not leave us be."
sentences.i: ...saying: "We sat idle and content — but our own curiosity gave us no peace."
sentences.n: The refrain is rhymed prose: bi-ṭūlinā / fuḍūlunā, both on -ūlinā; rhyme is pervasive in this text and is left visible here rather than smoothed away. وعاروا (ʿārū) is read as "they were overcome with shame, recoiled" (hollow verb عَارَ), which the same letters equally allow, rather than a form of عَرِيَ "be naked"; either fits a mourning-and-self-reproach scene, but "shame" ties directly to the curiosity confessed in the next breath.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا عَلَى هَذَا إِلَى قُرْبِ الصُّبْحِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū ʿalā hādhā ilā qurbi al-ṣubḥi
sentences.l: And they did not cease [being] thus until near dawn.
sentences.i: And they carried on so until near daybreak.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الشَّيْخُ وَسَخَّنَ لَهُمْ مَاءً فَغَسَلُوا وُجُوهَهُمْ وَلَبِسُوا أَثْوَابًا غَيْرَ الْأَوَّلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-shaykhu wa-sakhkhana lahum māʾan fa-ghasalū wujūhahum wa-labisū athwāban ghayra al-awwali
sentences.l: Then the old man rose and heated water for them, and they washed their faces and put on garments other than the first.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ ذَلِكَ يَا سَنَاهْ ذَهَبَ عَقْلِي وَحَارَ فِكْرِي وَاشْتَعَلَ سِرِّي وَنَسِيتُ مَا جَرَى عَلَيَّ وَلَمْ أَسْتَطِعِ السُّكُوتَ دُونَ أَنِّي كَلَّمْتُهُمْ وَسَأَلْتُهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytu dhālika yā sanāh dhahaba ʿaqlī wa-ḥāra fikrī wa-ishtaʿala sirrī wa-nasītu mā jarā ʿalayya wa-lam astaṭiʿi al-sukūta dūna annī kallamtuhum wa-saʾaltuhum
sentences.l: When I saw that, O Sanāh, my mind went, and my thought was bewildered, and my inner self blazed, and I forgot what had happened to me, and I could not bear silence without my speaking to them and questioning them.
sentences.i: When I saw that, my lady, I lost my wits, my thoughts reeled, and my heart caught fire; I forgot all that had befallen me, and I could not hold my tongue — I ended up speaking to them and questioning them.
sentences.n: يا سناه: an address to the lady of the house, the tale's present listener (this frame narrative has the qalandar telling his story to her). The printed letters (س-ن-ا-ه) do not match any word I know for "lady"; kept exactly as printed rather than emended to a form such as يا سِتّاه, and rendered "my lady" in the idiomatic layer on sense, not spelling.

sentences.t: وَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ أَيْشْ أَوْجَبَ هَذَا بَعْدَ انْشِرَاحِنَا وَتَعَبِنَا وَأَنْتُمْ بِحَمْدِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى فِيكُمْ عَقْلٌ تَامٌّ وَهَذِهِ الْأَفْعَالُ لَا يَفْعَلُهَا غَيْرُ الْمَجَانِينِ
sentences.tr: wa-qultu lahum aysh awjaba hādhā baʿda inshirāḥinā wa-taʿabinā wa-antum bi-ḥamdi Allāhi taʿālā fīkum ʿaqlun tāmmun wa-hādhihi al-afʿālu lā yafʿaluhā ghayru al-majānīni
sentences.l: And I said to them, "What has necessitated this, after our ease and our toil, when you — praise be to God the Exalted — have complete reason in you, and these deeds none does but madmen?"
sentences.i: And I said to them, "What has brought this on, after all our contentment and our labor? Praise God, you are men of perfect sense — yet these are things no one does but madmen!"
sentences.n: أَيْش (for the fuller أَيُّ شَيْء, "what") is a colloquial Middle Arabic contraction, common in direct speech in this text.

sentences.t: فَأَسْأَلُكُمْ بِأَعَزِّ الْأَشْيَاءِ عَلَيْكُمْ إِلَّا مَا قُلْتُمْ بِي خَبَرَكُمْ وَسَبَبَ قَلْعِ أَعْيُنِكُمْ وَسَخَامَةَ وُجُوهِكُمْ بِالرَّمَادِ وَالسَّوَادِ
sentences.tr: fa-asʾalukum bi-aʿazzi al-ashyāʾi ʿalaykum illā mā qultum bī khabarakum wa-sababa qalʿi aʿyunikum wa-sakhāmata wujūhikum bi-al-ramādi wa-al-sawādi
sentences.l: So I adjure you, by the dearest of things to you, will you not tell to-me your news, and the reason for the plucking-out of your eyes, and the sootiness of your faces with ash and blackness.
sentences.i: So I beg you, by all that is dearest to you, tell me your story — the reason your eyes were put out, and why your faces are blackened with ash and soot.
sentences.n: قلتم بي ("you told to-me", with بِـ where لِـ is expected) is this text's Middle Arabic use of بِـ as the preposition of the person told; kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتُوا وَقَالُوا لِي يَا فَتَى لَا يَغُرَّكَ شَبَابُكَ وَاعْدِلْ عَنْ سُؤَالِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafatū wa-qālū lī yā fatā lā yaghurraka shabābuka wa-iʿdil ʿan suʾālika
sentences.l: Then they turned and said to me, "O youth, do not let your youth deceive you, and turn away from your question."

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامُوا وَقُمْتُ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmū wa-qumtu maʿahum
sentences.l: Then they rose, and I rose with them.

sentences.t: فَقَدَّمَ الشَّيْخُ شَيْئًا مِنَ الْمَأْكُولِ فَبَعْدَ مَا أَكَلْنَا وَانْشَالَتِ الْأَوَانِي قَعَدُوا يَتَحَدَّثُونَ إِلَى أَنْ أَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ
sentences.tr: fa-qaddama al-shaykhu shayʾan min al-maʾkūli fa-baʿda mā akalnā wa-inshālati al-awānī qaʿadū yataḥaddathūna ilā an aqbala al-laylu
sentences.l: Then the old man served something of the food; and after we had eaten and the vessels were cleared away, they sat conversing until night came on.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الشَّيْخُ وَأَوْقَدَ الشُّمُوعَ وَالْقَنَادِيلَ وَقَدَّمَ لَنَا الْأَكْلَ وَالشُّرْبَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-shaykhu wa-awqada al-shumūʿa wa-al-qanādīla wa-qaddama lanā al-akla wa-al-shurba
sentences.l: Then the old man rose and lit the candles and the lamps, and served us food and drink.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغْنَا قَعَدْنَا لِلْمُحَادَثَةِ وَالْمُنَادَمَةِ إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghnā qaʿadnā li-al-muḥādathati wa-al-munādamati ilā niṣfi al-layli
sentences.l: When we had finished, we sat down for conversation and companionship until midnight.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشَّبَابُ لِلشَّيْخِ هَاتِ لَنَا رَاتِبَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shabābu li-al-shaykhi hāti lanā rātibanā
sentences.l: Then the young men said to the old man, "Bring us our ration."

sentences.t: فَقٰلَ جَاءَ وَقْتُ النَّوْمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla jāʾa waqtu al-nawmi
sentences.l: And he said, "The time of sleep has come."
sentences.n: قٰل again for قال, dagger-alif spelling as at P113L22; here unambiguously the old man, since he alone acts next.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الشَّيْخُ وَأَتَى بِالْأَطْبَاقِ وَفِيهِمُ الرَّمْلُ الْأَسْوَدُ فَفَعَلُوا مِثْلَ مَا فَعَلُوا أَوَّلَ لَيْلَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-shaykhu wa-atā bi-al-aṭbāqi wa-fīhimu al-ramlu al-aswadu fa-faʿalū mithla mā faʿalū awwala laylatin
sentences.l: Then the old man rose and brought the trays, with the black sand in them, and they did as they had done the first night.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا قَاعِدٌ عِنْدَهُمْ عَلَى هَذَا الْحَالِ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ وَهُمْ كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ يُسَخِّمُونَ وُجُوهَهُمْ بِالرَّمَادِ وَيَغْسِلُونَ وُجُوهَهُمْ وَيُغَيِّرُونَ أَثْوَابَهُمْ وَأَنَا أَتَعَجَّبُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَازْدَادَ وَسْوَاسِي بِحَيْثُ أَنِّي امْتَنَعْتُ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā qāʿidun ʿindahum ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli muddata shahrin wa-hum kulla laylatin yusakhkhimūna wujūhahum bi-al-ramādi wa-yaghsilūna wujūhahum wa-yughayyirūna athwābahum wa-anā ataʿajjabu min dhālika wa-izdāda waswāsī bi-ḥaythu annī imtanaʿtu min al-akli wa-al-shurbi
sentences.l: And I sat with them in this state for the space of a month, while every night they blackened their faces with ash, and washed their faces, and changed their garments, and I marveled at that, and my anxious brooding increased, to the point that I abstained from food and drink.
sentences.i: And so I stayed with them a full month, and every night they went on blackening their faces with ash, washing them clean, and changing their clothes, while I looked on in wonder and grew ever more unsettled, until I could no longer bring myself to eat or drink.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ أَيُّهَا الْفِتْيَانُ إِنْ لَمْ تُزِيلُوا هَمِّي وَتُخْبِرُونِي عَنْ سَبَبِ تَسْخِيمِ وُجُوهِكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahum ayyuhā al-fityānu in lam tuzīlū hammī wa-tukhbirūnī ʿan sababi taskhīmi wujūhikum
sentences.l: So I said to them, "O young men, if you do not remove my worry and tell me the reason for the blackening of your faces..."

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا كِتْمَانُ سِرِّنَا أَصْلَحُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū kitmānu sirrinā aṣlaḥu
sentences.l: And they said, "The concealing of our secret is more fitting."

sentences.t: فَبَقِيتُ مُتَحَيِّرًا فِي أُمُورِهِمْ وَأَنَا أَمْتَنِعُ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-baqītu mutaḥayyiran fī umūrihim wa-anā amtaniʿu min al-akli wa-al-shurbi
sentences.l: So I remained bewildered about their affairs, while I abstained from food and drink.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ لَا بُدَّأَنْ تُخْبِرُونِي مَا سَبَبُ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahum lā budda an tukhbirūnī mā sababu dhālika
sentences.l: I said to them, "It must be that you tell me what the reason for that is."
sentences.n: لا بدان is printed here as one continuous word (لا بُدَّ أَنْ run together, without even a hamza sign for أَنْ); kept as one token and vocalized so, though read as two words.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا هَذَا فِيهِ مَشَقَّةٌ عَلَيْكَ لِأَنَّكَ تَبْقَى مِثْلَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālū hādhā fīhi mashaqqatun ʿalayka li-annaka tabqā mithlanā
sentences.l: And they said, "There is hardship for you in this, because you will become like us."

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَابُدَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَإِلَّا دَعُونِي أُسَافِرُ مِنْ عِنْدِكُمْ إِلَى أَهْلِي وَأَسْتَرِيحُ مِنْ نَظَرِي مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَحْوَالِ وَالْمَثَلُ يَقُولُ بُعَادِي عَنْكُمْ أَجْمَلُ وَأَحْسَنُ عَيْنٌ لَا تَنْبَظِرُ قَلْبٌ لَا يَحْزَنُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā budda min dhālika wa-illā daʿūnī usāfiru min ʿindikum ilā ahlī wa-astarīḥu min naẓarī min hādhihi al-aḥwāli wa-al-mathalu yaqūlu buʿādī ʿankum ajmalu wa-aḥsanu ʿaynun lā tanbaẓiru qalbun lā yaḥzanu
sentences.l: And he said, "It must be so, or else let me travel away from you to my family and rest from my looking upon these doings; and the proverb says: my being far from you is more beautiful and better — an eye that does not see, a heart that does not grieve."
sentences.i: And he said, "It must be, or let me leave you and go home to my family, free of the sight of all this; as the proverb says: better my absence from you — the eye that sees nothing, the heart that grieves for nothing."
sentences.n: فقال keeps a third-person verb although the speaker is the narrator himself, who has otherwise used فقلت throughout this stretch — a momentary person-shift, kept as printed rather than normalized to فقلت. تنبظر is otherwise unattested; it is almost certainly a corruption of تُبْصِر in the common proverb عين لا تُبْصِر قلب لا يحزن ("an eye that doesn't see, a heart that doesn't grieve"), which is exactly the saying quoted here. Kept and vocalized as printed.

sentences.t: فَعَمِلُوا إِلَى كَبْشٍ ذَبَحُوهُ وَسَلَخُوهُ وَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿamilū ilā kabshin dhabaḥūhu wa-salakhūhu wa-
sentences.l: Then they went to [get] a ram; they slaughtered it and skinned it, and —
sentences.n: The sentence breaks off here mid-clause, as archived; the action continues in what follows.

sentences.t: قَالُوا لِي خُذْ هَذَا الْجِلْدَ مَعَكَ وَادْخُلْ فِي هَذَا الْجِلْدِ وَخَيِّطْهُ عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: qālū lī khudh hādhā al-jilda maʿaka wa-udkhul fī hādhā al-jildi wa-khayyiṭhu ʿalayka
sentences.l: They said to me, “Take this skin with you, and enter into this skin, and stitch it (shut) upon yourself,
sentences.i: They said to me, “Take this skin with you; get inside it, and sew it shut around you,

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ يَأْتِيكَ طَيْرٌ اسْمُهُ الرُّخُّ وَيَشِيلُكَ وَيَحُطُّكَ عَلَى جَبَلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu yaʾtīka ṭayrun ismuhu al-rukhkhu wa-yashīluka wa-yaḥuṭṭuka ʿalā jabalin
sentences.l: for there will come to you a bird, its name (is) the Rukh, and it will carry-you-off and set-you-down upon a mountain;
sentences.i: for a bird named the Rukh will come to you, and will carry you up and set you down on a mountain;
sentences.n: يَشِيلُ (from شَالَ, ‘to lift, carry’) is everyday colloquial vocabulary rather than the Classical حَمَلَ; this speech's diction stays plain and practical throughout.

sentences.t: فَشُقَّ الْجِلْدَ وَتَخْرُجُ مِنْهُ فَيَخَافُ مِنْكَ الطَّيْرُ فَيَرُوحُ وَيُخَلِّيكَ
sentences.tr: fa-shuqqa al-jilda wa-takhruju minhu fa-yakhāfu minka al-ṭayru fa-yarūḥu wa-yukhallīka
sentences.l: then tear the skin and come out of it, and the bird will fear you, and it will go off and leave-you (be);
sentences.i: then tear the skin open and climb out; the bird will take fright at you and fly off, leaving you there;
sentences.n: رَاحَ (‘go, depart’) and خَلَّى (‘leave, let be’) are both ordinary colloquial verbs, not elevated Classical diction.

sentences.t: فَامْشِ نِصْفَ نَهَارٍ تَلْقَي قُدَّامَكَ قَصْرًا غَرِيبَ الصِّفَةِ فَادْخُلْ فِيهِ وَقَدْ بَلَغْتَ مُنَاكَ
sentences.tr: fa-imshi niṣfa nahārin talqā quddāmaka qaṣran gharība al-ṣifati fa-udkhul fīhi wa-qad balaghta munāka
sentences.l: then walk half a day; you will find before you a palace strange of description; then enter into it, and you will (already) have reached your wish.
sentences.i: then walk on for half a day, and you will find before you a palace strange to look at; go inside it, and you will have gotten what you wished for.
sentences.n: قُدَّامَ (‘in front of’) is again colloquial, beside the Classical أَمَامَ. مُنَاكَ, ‘your wish’ (from مُنْيَة/مَنًى, a thing desired), is placed as if the wish were already granted the moment he goes in. تَلْقَي is printed with ي rather than the expected alif maqṣūra (تَلْقَى); this print does not always keep the two letters distinct word-finally, and the verb (from لَقِيَ, ‘to meet, find’) is read the same either way.

sentences.t: فَدُخُولُنَا إِلَى الْقَصْرِ هُوَ سَبَبُ سَخَامَةِ وُجُوهِنَا وَقَلْعِ عُيُونِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-dukhūlunā ilā al-qaṣri huwa sababu sakhāmati wujūhinā wa-qalʿi ʿuyūninā
sentences.l: As for our entering into the palace — it (is) the cause of the soot-blackening of our faces and the plucking-out of our eyes;
sentences.i: As for our entering that palace — it is the cause of our blackened faces, and of our eyes being torn out;
sentences.n: سَخَامَة, ‘soot-blackness,’ is the very thing behind the young men's nightly ritual of blackening their faces with ashes.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا نَحْنُ إِذَا حَكَيْنَا لَكَ يَطُولُ شَرْحُنَا فَإِنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ مِنَّا جَرَتْ لَهُ حِكَايَةٌ فِي قَلْعِ عَيْنِهِ الْيُمْنَى
sentences.tr: wa-ammā naḥnu idhā ḥakaynā laka yaṭūlu sharḥunā fa-inna kulla wāḥidin minnā jarat lahu ḥikāyatun fī qalʿi ʿaynihi al-yumnā
sentences.l: And as for us — if we were to tell (it) to you, our account would grow long, for each one of us — there befell him a story concerning the plucking-out of his right eye.”
sentences.i: As for us — if we told you our own story, the telling would run too long, for each of us has his own tale behind the loss of his right eye.”

sentences.t: فَفَرِحْتُ بِذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥtu bi-dhālika
sentences.l: And I rejoiced at that.
sentences.i: And I was glad of it.
sentences.n: The qalandar's gladness is a piece of dramatic irony: he does not yet know that this same road will cost him his own right eye in turn.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَعَلُوا بِي مَا قَالُوا
sentences.tr: thumma faʿalū bī mā qālū
sentences.l: Then they did to me what they had said.
sentences.i: Then they did with me as they had said.

sentences.t: وَحَمَلَنِي الطَّيْرُ وَحَطَّ بِي عَلَى الْجَبَلِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥamalanī al-ṭayru wa-ḥaṭṭa bī ʿalā al-jabali
sentences.l: And the bird carried me, and set (me), with me, down upon the mountain.
sentences.i: And the bird carried me off and set me down on the mountain.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْجِلْدِ وَ مَشَيْتُ حَتَّى دَخَلْتُ الْقَصْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu mina al-jildi wa-mashaytu ḥattā dakhaltu al-qaṣra
sentences.l: Then I came out of the skin, and I walked until I entered the palace.
sentences.i: Then I climbed out of the skin and walked on until I reached the palace and went in.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا فِيهِ أَرْبَعُونَ جَارِيَةً كَالْأَقْمَارِ لَا يَشْبَعُ مَنْ يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā fīhi arbaʿūna jāriyatan ka-al-aqmāri lā yashbaʿu man yanẓuru ilayhim
sentences.l: And behold, in it (were) forty maidens, like the moons — the one who looks at them cannot get his fill (of looking).
sentences.i: And there, inside, were forty maidens, lovely as moons, whom no one could ever look at enough.
sentences.n: إِلَيْهِمْ uses the masculine plural pronoun for the forty maidens, a feminine group; this text regularly levels feminine-plural agreement to the masculine form for groups of women — the first of several instances in this passage.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْنِي قَالُوا كُلُّهُمْ أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا بِكَ وَمَرْحَبًا يَا مَوْلَانَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawnī qālū kulluhum ahlan wa-sahlan bika wa-marḥaban yā mawlānā
sentences.l: And when they saw me, they said, all of them, “Welcome and ease to you, and greetings, O our master!
sentences.i: When they saw me, they all cried out, “Welcome, and welcome again, O our lord!
sentences.n: Again masculine-plural رَأَوْنِي / قَالُوا / كُلُّهُمْ for the forty maidens, matching إِلَيْهِمْ just above; this leveling runs throughout the passage and will not be flagged at every occurrence.

sentences.t: وَنَحْنُ لَنَا شَهْرٌ فِي انْتِظَارِكَ فَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَتَانَا لِمَا يَسْتَحِقُّنَا وَ نَسْتَحِقُّهُ
sentences.tr: wa-naḥnu lanā shahrun fī intiẓārika fa-al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī atānā li-mā yastaḥiqqunā wa-nastaḥiqquhu
sentences.l: and we have had a month in the waiting-for-you; so praise (be) to God, who has brought us to what deserves-us and (what) we deserve-it.”
sentences.i: We have been a whole month awaiting you — so praise be to God, who has brought us one who deserves us and whom we deserve.”
sentences.n: لِمَا يَسْتَحِقُّنَا وَنَسْتَحِقُّهُ, literally ‘to what deserves us and we deserve it,’ means the qalandar himself: the two sides are a fitting match.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ أَجْلَسُونِي عَلَى مَرْتَبَةٍ عَالِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum ajlasūnī ʿalā martabatin ʿāliyatin
sentences.l: Then, indeed, they seated me upon a high dais.
sentences.i: Then they seated me upon a high divan.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا أَنْتَ الْيَوْمَ سَيِّدُنَا وَالْحَاكِمُ عَلَيْنَا وَنَحْنُ جَوَارِكَ وَتَحْتَ طَاعَتِكَ فَأْمُرْ فِينَا بِحُكْمِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū anta al-yawma sayyidunā wa-al-ḥākimu ʿalaynā wa-naḥnu jawārika wa-taḥta ṭāʿatika fa-ʾmur fīnā bi-ḥukmika
sentences.l: And they said, “You (are) today our lord and the ruler over us, and we (are) your slave-girls, and under your obedience; so command concerning us by your judgment.”
sentences.i: And they said, “Today you are our lord and ruler; we are your handmaids, and yours to command — so give us your orders as you see fit.”
sentences.n: جَوَارِكَ, ‘your slave-girls,’ is a possessive phrase doing the work of a predicate: ‘we are [your slave-girls].’

sentences.t: فَعَجِبْتُ مِنْ أَحْوَالِهِنَّ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿajibtu min aḥwālihinna
sentences.l: And I marveled at their (f.) state(s).
sentences.i: And I marveled at their condition.
sentences.n: Here the text reverts to the expected feminine-plural pronoun -hinna, unlike إِلَيْهِمْ / كُلُّهُمْ above — the leveling toward masculine-plural agreement is not a fixed rule for this speaker, only a frequent tendency.

sentences.t: وَأَتَوْنِي بِطَعَامٍ فَأَكَلْتُ أَنَا وَإِيَّاهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-atawnī bi-ṭaʿāmin fa-akaltu anā wa-iyyāhum
sentences.l: And they came to me with food, and I ate, I and them (together).
sentences.i: And they brought me food, and I ate together with them.
sentences.n: وَإِيَّاهُمْ, literally ‘and them,’ uses the independent object pronoun coordinated after a verb whose subject is already أَنَا; it is the idiom for ‘along with them.’

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمُوا لِي الشَّرَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-qaddamū lī al-sharāba
sentences.l: And they served to me the drink.
sentences.i: And they served me wine.

sentences.t: وَاجْتَمَعْنَ حَوْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-ijtamaʿna ḥawlī
sentences.l: And they (f.) gathered around me.
sentences.i: And they gathered around me.
sentences.n: اجْتَمَعْنَ correctly takes the feminine-plural ending here, unlike the masculine forms just before and after it.

sentences.t: وَقَامُوا خَمْسَةٌ فَرَشُوا حَصِيرَةً وَرَحَّبُوا حَوْلَهَا مِنَ الْمَشْمُومِ وَالْفَوَاكِهِ وَالنُّقْلِ أَشْيَاءَ كَثِيرَةً
sentences.tr: wa-qāmū khamsatun fa-rashū ḥaṣīratan wa-raḥḥabū ḥawlahā mina al-mashmūmi wa-al-fawākihi wa-al-nuqli ashyāʾa kathīratan
sentences.l: And five (of them) rose, and spread out a mat, and made-wide around it, of the sweet-smelling herbs and the fruits and the dried-fruits, many things,
sentences.i: And five of them got up and spread out a mat, and set out around it a great many things — fragrant herbs, fruit, and dried fruit —
sentences.n: رَحَّبُوا ordinarily means ‘welcomed’ (someone, with بِـ); here it instead takes حَوْلَهَا, ‘around it,’ so it is read in its more literal sense — ‘made wide, made ample’ (from رَحُبَ, ‘to be spacious’) — i.e. spread things generously around the mat. خَمْسَةٌ, the form used for masculine-counted nouns, counts the (implicitly feminine) maidens here — one more instance of this text's loose gender agreement.

sentences.t: وَأَحْضَرُوا إِلَيْهِ الْمُدَامَ
sentences.tr: wa-aḥḍarū ilayhi al-mudāma
sentences.l: and they brought to it the wine.
sentences.i: and brought the wine to it.
sentences.n: الْمُدَام, ‘wine’ (literally ‘the lasting one’), is a Classical poetic epithet for wine used here as a plain noun.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسْنَا لِلشَّرَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasnā li-al-sharābi
sentences.l: Then we sat down for the drink.
sentences.i: Then we sat down to drink.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذُوا عُودًا وَغَنَّوْا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhū ʿūdan wa-ghannaw ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And they took up a lute, and sang upon it.
sentences.i: And they took up a lute and sang to it.

sentences.t: وَدَارَتِ الْكُؤُسُ وَالطَّاسَاتُ بَيْنَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-dārati al-kuʾūsu wa-al-ṭāsātu baynanā
sentences.l: And the cups, and the bowls, went round between us,
sentences.i: and the cups, and the bowls, passed from hand to hand among us,
sentences.n: الطَّاسَات (sg. طَاسَة, ‘bowl, cup’) is a Persian loanword naturalized into Arabic; دَارَتِ agrees with the nearer of the two coordinated subjects, as Classical usage allows.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ عَلَىَّ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ مَا أَنْسَانِي هُمُومَ الدُّنْيَا جَمِيعَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala ʿalayya mina al-faraḥi mā ansānī humūma al-dunyā jamīʿahā
sentences.l: And there entered upon me, of the joy, that which made-me-forget the cares of the world, all of it.
sentences.i: And such joy came over me that it made me forget all the cares of the world.
sentences.n: Printed عَلَى with alif maqṣūra rather than the fuller عَلَيَّ, but the sense (“there came over me…”) requires ʿalayya, ‘upon me’; this print does not always keep the spellings of ʿalā and ʿalayya distinct.

sentences.t: وَقُلْتُ هَذَا هُوَ الْعَيْشُ
sentences.tr: wa-qultu hādhā huwa al-ʿayshu
sentences.l: And I said, “This — it (is) the life!”
sentences.i: And I said, “This is truly living!”

sentences.t: وَلَا زِلْتُ مَعَهُمْ حَتَّى وَقْتِ الْمَنَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā ziltu maʿahum ḥattā waqti al-manāmi
sentences.l: And I did not cease (to be) with them until the time of sleep.
sentences.i: And I stayed on with them until it was time to sleep.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا خُذْ مَعَكَ مَا تَخْتَارُ مِنَّا تَنَامُ عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū khudh maʿaka mā takhtāru minnā tanāmu ʿindaka
sentences.l: And they said, “Take with you whichever (one) you choose of us, to sleep beside you.”
sentences.i: And they said, “Take with you whichever of us you choose, to sleep at your side.”
sentences.n: مَا تَخْتَارُ, literally ‘what/whichever you choose,’ functions like a personal relative (‘whoever’), a common use of مَا in this text.

sentences.t: فَاخْتَارَتْ وَاحِدَةٌ مِنْهُنَّ مَلِيحَةُ الْوَجْهِ كَحِيلَةُ الطَّرْفِ دَعْجَةُ الشَّعْرِ فَلَمْجَةُ الثَّغْرِ كَامِلَةُ الْفُنُونِ بِحَاجِبٍ مَقْرُونٍ كَأَنَّهَا خَوْطَانِ أَوْ قَضِيبُ رَيْحَانٍ تُدْهِشُ وَتُحَيِّرُ الْخَاطِرَ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-ikhtārat wāḥidatun minhunna malīḥatu al-wajhi kaḥīlatu al-ṭarfi daʿjatu al-shaʿri falamjatu al-thaghri kāmilatu al-funūni bi-ḥājibin maqrūnin ka-annahā khawṭāni aw qaḍību rayḥānin tudhishu wa-tuḥayyiru al-khāṭira kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And one of them chose (herself) — beautiful of face, kohl-lidded of glance, raven-dark of hair, [uncertain] of mouth, perfect in accomplishments, with a joined eyebrow, as though she were two slender boughs, or a sprig of sweet basil, bewildering and confounding the mind — as the poet said of her:
sentences.i: And one of them chose herself — a girl beautiful of face, dark-eyed as though rimmed with kohl, raven-haired, [uncertain] of mouth, accomplished in every art, her eyebrows meeting as one, as though she were two green boughs, or a spray of basil, enough to bewilder any mind — as the poet said of her:
sentences.n: فَلَمْجَةُ الثَّغْرِ is obscure: the root ل-م-ج is not attested in this sense. Given the run of stock beauty-epithets for the mouth, the likeliest intent is لَمْيَاء الثَّغْر, ‘dark-lipped,’ or فَلْجَاء الثَّغْر, ‘gap-toothed’ (both classical praise-terms for a mouth) — but neither matches the printed consonants exactly, and the word may simply be corrupt. It is vocalized as printed and translated only by context. حَاجِبٍ مَقْرُونٍ, ‘a joined eyebrow’ (eyebrows meeting above the nose), is a mark of beauty here, not a flaw. دَعْجَةُ الشَّعْرِ transfers دَعَج — properly the intense blackness of a wide, dark eye — onto the hair; the extension is unusual but the sense (raven-black hair) is clear.

sentences.t:
نُشَبِّهُ بِالْغُصْنِ الرَّطِيبِ جَهَالَةً * وَحَاشَا مَعَايِنَهَا نُشَبِّهُ بِالظِّبَى
مِنْ أَيْنَ لِلظَّبْيِ الْعَزِيزِ قَوَامُهَا * وَمَشْرَبُهَا الْمَعْسُولُ طَابَتْ مَشْرَبَا
وَأَعْيُنُهَا النُّجْلُ الْقَوَاتِلُ فِي الْهَوَى * سَبَيْنَ الْقَتِيلَ الْمُسْتَهَامَ الْمُعَذَّبَا
صَبَوْتُ إِلَيْهَا صَبْوَةً جَاهِلِيَّةً * وَلَا عَجَبَ لِلْمُدْنَفِ الصَّبِّ إِنْ صَبَا
sentences.tr:
nushabbihu bi-al-ghuṣni al-raṭībi jahālatan * wa-ḥāshā maʿāyinahā nushabbihu bi-al-ẓibā
min ayna li-al-ẓabyi al-ʿazīzi qawāmuhā * wa-mashrabuhā al-maʿsūlu ṭābat mashraban
wa-aʿyunuhā al-nujlu al-qawātilu fī al-hawā * sabayna al-qatīla al-mustahāma al-muʿadhdhabā
ṣabawtu ilayhā ṣabwatan jāhiliyyatan * wa-lā ʿajaba li-al-mudnafi al-ṣabbi in ṣabā
sentences.l:
We liken [her], out of ignorance, to the moist bough — * but far be it, her eyes we should liken to gazelles!
From where could the precious gazelle get her stature? * and her honeyed drinking-place — she has grown sweet as a drinking-place.
And her wide, deadly eyes, in love, * have taken captive the slain one, the love-maddened, the tormented.
I yearned for her with a reckless yearning — * and no wonder, if the wasted, love-sick one should yearn.
sentences.i:
We compare her, out of ignorance, to the green bough — * but heaven forbid we compare her eyes to a gazelle's!
How could any gazelle, however prized, match her figure? * and how sweet her mouth is to drink from!
Her wide, deadly eyes have taken captive, in love, * the slain, love-crazed, tormented lover.
I gave my heart to her with a wild, reckless passion — * small wonder, if the wasted, love-sick man should love.
sentences.n: The rhyme runs on -ā throughout (bi-al-ẓibā / mashrabā / al-muʿadhdhabā / in ṣabā). بِالظِّبَى is printed without the medial alif and final hamza that الظِّبَاء, ‘gazelles,’ would properly take — a common defective spelling for this plural in the edition; a reading الظُّبَى, ‘the sword-blades’ (pl. of ظُبَة), is also possible from the bare consonants, but ‘gazelles’ fits the poem's argument (that she outdoes the stock gazelle-comparison) and is picked up explicitly by الظَّبْيِ, ‘the gazelle,’ in the next line. جَاهِلِيَّة here is not literally ‘of the Jāhiliyya’ but the idiom for a reckless, headlong passion.

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَلْتُهَا قَوْلَ الْقَائِلِ
sentences.tr: wa-anshaltuhā qawla al-qāʾili
sentences.l: And I recited to her the saying of the sayer:
sentences.i: And I recited to her the words of the poet:
sentences.n: Printed أَنْشَلْتُهَا, with ل, has no sense from the root ن-ش-ل (‘to snatch out’); both the meaning required here and the parallel formula used elsewhere in this text (كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ) point to أَنْشَدْتُهَا, ‘I recited to her’ (from أَنْشَدَ, ‘to recite verse’) — very likely a one-letter misprint (ل for د). It is vocalized as printed and translated by the sense the context requires.

sentences.t:
عَيْنِي لِغَيْرِ جَمَالِكُمْ لَا تَنْظُرُ * وَسِوَاكُمْ فِي خَاطِرِي لَا يَخْطُرُ
وَجَمِيعُ فِكْرِي فِي هَوَاكُمْ سَادَتِي * وَعَلَى مَحَبَّتِكُمْ أَمُوتُ وَأُحْشَرُ
sentences.tr:
ʿaynī li-ghayri jamālikum lā tanẓuru * wa-siwākum fī khāṭirī lā yakhṭuru
wa-jamīʿu fikrī fī hawākum sādatī * wa-ʿalā maḥabbatikum amūtu wa-uḥsharu
sentences.l:
My eye looks not upon any beauty but yours; * and none but you crosses my mind.
And all my thought is in your love, my masters; * and upon your love I shall die and be raised again.
sentences.i:
My eyes look on no beauty but yours; * and nothing but you ever crosses my mind.
All my thoughts are bound up in loving you, my lords; * and in love of you I shall die, and rise again.
sentences.n: The poem addresses the beloved with the plural ـكُمْ and سَادَتِي, ‘my masters’ — a conventional plural of respect for a single beloved, not a plural of number. أُحْشَرُ, ‘I shall be gathered/raised’ (on the Day of Judgment), turns the lover's vow into a mock-religious oath.

sentences.t: فَقُمْتُ وَنِمْتُ لَيْلَةً مَعَهَا مَا رَأَيْتُ أَحْسَنَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qumtu wa-nimtu laylatan maʿahā mā raʾaytu aḥsana minhā
sentences.l: Then I got up, and slept a night with her; I had not seen (anyone) more beautiful than her.
sentences.i: Then I rose and spent the night with her — I had never seen anyone more beautiful.
sentences.n: فَقُمْتُ, ‘then I rose (from the reciting),’ picks the narration back up after the verse quotation.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَتْ دَخَلْنَ بِي الْحَمَّامَ فَغَسَّلُونِي وَأَلْبَسُونِي مِنْ أَفْخَرِ الثِّيَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥat dakhalna bī al-ḥammāma fa-ghassalūnī wa-albasūnī min afkhari al-thiyābi
sentences.l: And when it became morning, they (f.) took me into the bath, and washed me, and clothed me in the finest of the garments,
sentences.i: And when morning came, they took me to the bath and washed me, and dressed me in the finest clothes,
sentences.n: دَخَلْنَ keeps the feminine-plural ending, but غَسَّلُونِي وَأَلْبَسُونِي switch straight back to masculine-plural forms for the same women — the same leveling seen in إِلَيْهِمْ / قَالُوا above.

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمُوا لَنَا الْأَكْلَ فَأَكَلْنَا وَالشَّرَابَ فَشَرِبْنَا
sentences.tr: wa-qaddamū lanā al-akla fa-akalnā wa-al-sharāba fa-sharibnā
sentences.l: and they served to us the food, so we ate, and the drink, so we drank.
sentences.i: and served us food, which we ate, and wine, which we drank.

sentences.t: وَدَارَتِ الْكُؤُسُ بَيْنَنَا إِلَى اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-dārati al-kuʾūsu baynanā ilā al-layli
sentences.l: And the cups went round between us until the night.
sentences.i: And the cups went round among us until nightfall.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اخْتَرْتُ مِنْهُنَّ وَاحِدَةً مَلِيحَةَ الْأَوْصَافِ لَيِّنَةَ الْأَعْطَافِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: thumma ikhtartu minhunna wāḥidatan malīḥata al-awṣāfi layyinata al-aʿṭāfi kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: Then I chose from among them one, beautiful of attributes, supple of sides, as the poet said of her:
sentences.i: Then I chose one of them, lovely in every feature and supple and graceful in figure, as the poet said of her:

sentences.t: حَيْثُ يَقُولُ —
sentences.tr: ḥaythu yaqūlu —
sentences.l: where he says—
sentences.i: As he says—

sentences.t:
رَأَيْتُ فِي صَدْرِهَا حُقّانِ قَدْ خُتِمَا * بِمِسْكَةٍ تَمْنَعُ الْعُشَّاقَ ضَمَّهُمَا
تَحْرُسُهُمَا بِسِهَامٍ مِنْ لَوَاحِظِهَا * مَنْ يَعْتَدِيهَا أَصَابَتْهُ بِسَهْمَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr:
ra'aytu fī ṣadrihā ḥuqqāni qad khutimā * bi-miskatin tamna'u al-'ushshāqa ḍammahumā
taḥrusuhumā bi-sihāmin min lawāḥiẓihā * man ya'tadīhā aṣābat-hu bi-sahmayhimā
sentences.l:
I saw in her bosom two caskets [that] were sealed * with a musk-seal that forbids lovers their embracing
she guards them both with arrows from her glances * whoever transgresses against her, [the arrows] strike him with their two arrows
sentences.i: I saw in her breast two sealed caskets, sealed with a mole of musk that keeps lovers from ever embracing them; she guards them with arrows shot from her glances—whoever assails her, those two arrows strike him down.
sentences.n: The image: the beloved's breasts as two sealed caskets (ḥuqqān), their “seal” a dark, musk-coloured mole; her glances are guarding arrows. "بِسَهْمَيْهِمَا" ("with their two arrows") most likely refers back to the pair of eyes implied by "لواحظها" (her glances), not to the caskets themselves.

sentences.t: فَنِمْتُ عِنْدَهَا بِأَجْمَلِ لَيْلَةٍ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-nimtu 'indahā bi-ajmali laylatin ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: So I slept beside her the most-beautiful of a night, until the morning.
sentences.i: So I slept beside her through the most beautiful of nights, until morning.

sentences.t: وَبِالِاخْتِصَارِ يَا سَيِّدَتَاهْ أَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهُنَّ فِي أَرْغَلِ عَيْشٍ مُدَّةَ سَنَةٍ كَامِلَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-bi-al-ikhtiṣāri yā sayyidatāh aqamtu 'indahunna fī arghali 'ayshin muddata sanatin kāmilatin
sentences.l: And, in the abridging, O my-lady, I stayed with them in a most-arghal living, [for] the space of a complete year.
sentences.i: And, in short, O my lady, I stayed with them in the most comfortable of lives, for the space of a full year.
sentences.n: "سَيِّدَتَاهْ" is the exclamatory-vocative form (نداء الندبة/الاختصاص): سَيِّدَة + alif + pausal hā', "O my lady!"—the qalandar addressing the lady of the house as he narrates. "أَرْغَل" is printed with lām where the expected word is أَرْغَد (arghad, "most pleasant/comfortable", the ordinary phrase أَرْغَد عَيْش); the letters د and ل are otherwise unrelated in shape, but this exact substitution recurs twice more later in this night (see "أَنْشَلَتْ", "وَجِلْتُ"), so it looks like a genuine, repeated feature of this archive page rather than a one-off. Kept as printed and vocalised for the sense the passage plainly intends.

sentences.t: وَفِي رَأْسِ السَّنَةِ قُلْنَ لِي لَيْتَنَا مَاعَرَفْنَاكَ فَإِنْ سَمِعْتَ مِنَّا كَانَ فِيهِ صَلَاحُ حَالِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-fī ra'si al-sanati qulna lī laytanā mā 'arafnāka fa-in sami'ta minnā kāna fīhi ṣalāḥu ḥālika
sentences.l: And at the head of the year they (f.) said to me: would-that we-did-not-know-you, for if you heard from us, there-was in-it the-soundness-of your-condition.
sentences.i: And at the year's end they said to me: would that we had never known you—for if you heed us, it will be for your own good.

sentences.t: وَصَارُوا يَبْكُونَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārū yabkūna
sentences.l: And they fell to weeping.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبْتُ وَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ مَا الْخَبَرُ
sentences.tr: fa-ta'ajjabtu wa-qultu lahum mā al-khabaru
sentences.l: So I marvelled, and I said to them: what is the news?
sentences.i: So I was astonished, and I said to them, “What is the matter?”

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا إِنَّنَا نَحْنُ بَنَاتُ مُلُوكٍ وَنَحْنُ مُجْتَمِعِينَ هُنَا مُدَّةَ سِنِينَ نَغِيبُ أَرْبَعِينَ يَوْمًا وَنَقْعُدُ سَنَةً نَأْكُلُ وَ نَشْرَبُ وَنَلَذُّ وَنَطْرَبُ ثُمَّ نَغِيبُ وَهَٰذَا دَأْبُنَا
